post.summary:
Per-pick post-mortem for Episode 1 (picked Oct 2, measured to the Oct 8 close). Equal-weighted, the five picks averaged -3.3% (+10.3, -1.5, -5.5, -8.5, -11.2) while the S&P 500 rose 0.55%, so they trailed by about 3.8 points. Without MPC the average was -6.7%.

**What the pre-pick data got right**
- **Stretched stocks did worst.** The two picks most stretched above their 50-day were the two worst: TWLO (~30% above, -8.5%) and MTRN (~25% above, -11.2%).
- **A big pop with no news reversed.** MTRN had jumped 16% in two days with no news and only about 1.1-1.3x normal volume.
- **Timing the index add was wrong for TWLO.** Its S&P 500 inclusion took effect at the start of the episode week, so the forced buying was already used up. Fact-checkers had flagged the extension gate and recommended swapping in TER, but the panel kept TWLO.
- **The winner had a fresh, real catalyst and a sector-wide trend.** MPC (+10.3%) was 16% above its 50-day, its pop came on concrete fuel-shortage news, and all the big refiners were rising together. That pattern (stocks keep drifting after news-driven moves, and whole industries trend together) is a documented effect. The G7 diesel-reserve release that the dossier flagged as MPC's main risk did not bite, because crude rose above $102. That part was luck.
- **NVDA and CHEF were the least stretched (~7% each) and lost the least among the losers** (-1.5% and -5.5%). Neither hit its buy trigger, and both stayed above their invalidation levels.
- **The week's damage came from one shared factor.** Three or four of the five picks were exposed to AI/semis or to rising rates on high-valuation stocks. The week's shock hit exactly that: a report that OpenAI's revenue (~$50B annualized) was below estimates, plus rising yields. NVDA's dossier had even listed its OpenAI exposure as a risk.

**What was noise or unknown**
- Price above the analyst consensus target did not separate winners from losers: MPC, the best pick, was about 11% above its target.
- Volume data mostly wasn't available, so it couldn't separate anything.
- TWLO insider selling was never sourced.
- How the alternates did is unknown, because outcome data wasn't provided and the search budget went to MTRN, TWLO and MPC.

**How much to trust this**
With n=5 and picks that moved together, there are really only about two independent bets: energy versus AI/rates. The rank correlation between extension and return is about -0.5, which is not significant at n=5 (p around 0.35).

**Lessons that match published research, and should be backtested before adoption**
- A cap on how far a pick can sit above its 50-day.
- A filter on sharp one- or two-day pops that have no news behind them.
- An index-event rule, so a stock isn't picked the week its inclusion takes effect.
- A limit on how many picks share the same theme or factor.
- Fixes to how results are measured.

**Gaps in the record**
- The panel's ballots and decision are not stored in dossier.json. The only trace of the override is the "PRODUCER FLAG" text in TWLO's risks.
- MPC's reference price is the Oct 1 close, while the other picks use Oct 2, which is not apples-to-apples. The backtester measures from the next session's open (Oct 5).

**Web searches (4 used)**
- One search confirmed TWLO's post-inclusion profit-taking (Weiss alert: down 5.69% intraday Tuesday to $283.79 from a $300.91 Monday close).
- Searches for what drove MTRN's drop and for MPC's Mizuho target raise found nothing dated October 2026, so those two remain unverified.

findings.title: Overall result: -3.3% equal-weight vs S&P +0.55%; one winner on a different factor
findings.detail: Equal-weight return of the 5 picks = (10.3 - 1.5 - 5.5 - 8.5 - 11.2) / 5 = -3.28%, against +0.55% for the SPX. That is about -3.8 points of underperformance. Excluding MPC, the other four averaged -6.7%. MPC was the only pick exposed to oil and refining cracks. The other four were exposed, to varying degrees, to the week's shock: AI/semis plus rising yields hitting high-valuation stocks (the OpenAI annualized revenue of ~$50B came in below estimates, while yields and oil rose). The Nasdaq Composite was flat, so the week's split was inside the market: AI-linked names down, energy up. Most of the spread between the picks is explained by factor exposure, not stock-specific skill.

findings.title: MPC (+10.3%): the pre-pick data that lined up was a fresh, fundamental catalyst plus industry momentum, with moderate extension
findings.detail: At the pick, MPC was about 16% above its 50-day (about $363) and 61% above its 200-day. It was moderately extended, below the 25-30% levels of TWLO and MTRN. Its 1-day move into the pick (+6.25% on Oct 1) was as large as MTRN's daily moves, but it came on concrete fundamental news: the EU diesel shortage, China halting fuel exports, EIA distillate draws, and management at UBS saying inventories were severely depleted. MPC, VLO, DINO and PSX had all logged 6 straight weekly gains, so this was an industry-wide trend, not one stock. It was about 2.5% under its $431 high, with a defined pivot. The stock was ~11% ABOVE the average analyst target (mid-$370s), but the Street-high targets were rising (Goldman $472, Raymond James $445), and price above consensus did not stop a +10% week. The main risk named in the dossier (G7/IEA diesel release, diesel futures slumping Oct 2) did NOT play out, because crude rose above $102 on the Middle East situation. That part of the win is macro luck, not a signal the system read. Measurement caveat: MPC's reference is the Oct 1 close (420.15). The Oct 2 close was never confirmed (dossier do_not_say), so its +10.3% includes an unknown Friday move and is not comparable to the other picks. Rules-based view: it broke the $431 pivot, so a trigger-follower who entered near $431 made about +7.5% to $463.34.

findings.implication: Weight news-driven moves above no-news moves, and value industry-wide momentum (several stocks in the same industry trending together). Both are documented effects: Chan 2003, 'Stock price reaction to news and no-news'; Moskowitz & Grinblatt 1999, industry momentum. Keep a non-AI theme slot for diversification. Do NOT conclude that 'price above analyst consensus is fine' from one stock.

findings.title: MTRN (-11.2%): extension plus a 16% no-news, low-volume 2-day pop; even the trigger-follower lost
findings.detail: The pre-pick data had nearly every warning sign. It was about 25% above its 50-day ($250) and 40% above its 200-day. It had run about 16% in 2 sessions (+6% Thursday, +9.5% Friday). The dossier says no company news explained the pop ('our read' that it rode semis strength). Volume was only about 1.1-1.3x average. It sat above the $310 consensus target, with only Jefferies' $314 higher. Valuation was about 45x guidance, with a GAAP P/E near 71. The dossier itself said 'this move takes back the August high rather than breaking out of a long base.' Path: Mon Oct 5 hit an all-time high around $325 and closed $319.18, so it TRIGGERED the $314 breakout rule. Implied closes were about $312 on Tue, about $291 on Wed (-6.9%) and $277.11 on Thu (-4.7%), below the $285 invalidation. A listener following the show's own trigger bought near $319 and was stopped at about $277: -13%. Its link to chips (it sells into semis) gave it exposure to the AI selloff on Wed-Thu.
findings.evidence: dossier.json picks[MTRN] facts ('No company news explained Friday's pop', 'only modestly above average', 'about 25% above its 50-day'); candidate_dossiers.json MTRN verdict ('now past the 15-20% extension guideline'). Web search found no MTRN-specific news for Oct 6-8, 2026 (consistent with a factor/reversal move, but unconfirmed).
findings.implication: Strongest lesson, and consistent with known effects: short-term reversal (Jegadeesh 1990; Lehmann 1990), reversal of big no-news moves (Chan 2003), and the lottery/MAX effect, where stocks with extreme recent daily returns underperform (Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw 2011). Add a gate: skip names whose 2-day return exceeds about 10% (or about 3x ATR14) when there is no fundamental news, and cap extension above the 50-day at about 20%. Also, do not treat a breakout trigger as valid when the stock is already 20%+ extended. Backtest both rules in src/watchlist/backtest before adopting them.

findings.title: TWLO (-8.5%): the panel overrode the extension gate, and the index-event timing was predictably bad
findings.detail: Pre-pick red flags: (1) Extension of about 28-35% above the 50-day. Both fact-checks said this met the show's '30%+ above the 50-day' drop rule and recommended swapping in TER. The panel kept TWLO anyway. (2) Event timing: the S&P 500 inclusion took effect before the open on Tue Oct 6. The forced buying landed at Monday's close, so the whole episode week came after the demand shock. It was also a migration from the S&P MidCap 400, so mid-cap index funds were selling, which shrinks net flow. (3) Friday's bar tagged $306 and closed about $5 off the high on an $18 range, so sellers were showing up. (4) It traded ~13% above the ~$263 consensus target, and HSBC had downgraded it to Reduce with a $211 target on Sep 25 (unconfirmed pre-pick, but reported by Weiss afterwards). (5) The organic growth guide was only 11-12% after a near-tripling. Path: Monday close $300.91, essentially flat to Friday's $301.27, so the inclusion buying did not even lift the price. Tuesday traded down 5.7% intraday to $283.79. Wednesday closed $273, below the $280 invalidation. Thursday $275.77. Rate-sensitive, high-multiple software also suffered from rising yields that week.
findings.evidence: dossier.json picks[TWLO] risks[0] ('PRODUCER FLAG, EXTENSION GATE ... both recommend swapping in TER'), risks[1] (sell-the-news), risks[2] (Friday reversal); Weiss Ratings alert https://weissratings.com/en/instant-news-alerts/twilio-inc-twlo-down-5-7-should-i-harvest-this-position (attributes the drop to profit-taking after inclusion; cites HSBC Reduce $211).
findings.implication: Consistent with known effects: price gains from S&P 500 inclusion now happen mostly between the announcement and the effective date, and partly reverse afterwards, with the overall effect much smaller than it used to be (Greenwood & Sammon 2022, 'The Disappearing Index Effect'; Patel & Welch 2017). Add an event-calendar rule: do not pick a name whose index-inclusion effective date falls inside, or just before, the episode week. Make the 50-day extension gate hard: an override must be logged with a reason and tracked. Whether TER would have done better is unknown, since TER is also semis/AI-exposed, so do not claim the override cost the show a specific amount.

findings.title: NVDA (-1.5%): a weak breakout and thin buzz; trigger never fired; AI/OpenAI exposure was flagged in the dossier
findings.detail: Pre-pick: a cleaner chart than the others, only about 7% above a rising 50-day ($218) after a 4-month base. But the breakout was one day old and closed about 1.6% below the $238 intraday high, just under the prior intraday record near $236. Volume was only about 10% above average, and Stocktwits buzz was 'normal', with neutral sentiment ('returning', not 'surging'). That is weak evidence for a social-buzz slot. Price was about 37% below the average analyst target, but that did not help. The dossier explicitly listed 'Circular AI money' (the completed $30B OpenAI commitment), and the week's shock was an OpenAI revenue report: -2.9% on Oct 8. The Oct 7 close of about $237.47 was just under the $238 trigger, so a rules-follower never entered. The stock held above the $218 invalidation, so the setup is intact.
findings.evidence: dossier.json picks[NVDA] facts (volume about 135M vs about 124M avg; Stocktwits 'neutral', 'normal'), risks (circular AI money; 'Episode balance ... semis-heavy'); results note (Oct 7 close about $237.47, -2.9% on Oct 8 after the OpenAI revenue report).

(a) The social slot's buzz evidence was thin; require measurable mention acceleration (as the code's social_score intends) rather than 'normal chatter'. (b) NVDA added a third or fourth AI-linked pick. The dossier itself warned the episode was semis-heavy.

findings.title: CHEF (-5.5%): the least extended pick pulled back to its 50-day; the setup is intact; mostly noise
findings.detail: Pre-pick: about 7% above a rising 50-day near $110, a breakout from a month-long base, no recent dilution or downgrades, and low buzz. These were the textbook sleeper traits. Weaknesses: the breakout was unconfirmed (closed $117.94, below the $118.51 intraday high, and no volume data was found). It traded at about 47x earnings, right at the average target. It is discretionary and rate-sensitive, and the dossier flagged diesel delivery costs as a risk: oil and yields both rose that week. The trigger ($118.50 close) never fired. The only process lesson is that breakout picks without volume data should go out as 'watch for trigger', which is what the show did. Score on trigger and invalidation rules, not on close-to-close returns.

findings.title: Extension vs outcome: right direction, not statistically meaningful at n=5
findings.detail: Extension above the 50-day at the pick, versus return: NVDA 7% / -1.5, CHEF 7% / -5.5, MPC 16% / +10.3, MTRN 25% / -11.2, TWLO ~30% / -8.5. On its own data, though, the sample cannot separate extension from the AI/rates factor, because both extended losers were also AI- or duration-exposed.

No pattern, and the literature on target-implied returns is weak. Volume confirmation: mostly missing (only NVDA's +10% and MTRN's 1.1-1.3x were known), so it can't be judged; it should come from the quant scan. Insider selling: TWLO's ~$134M was never sourced (do_not_say), so it can't be evaluated. The G7 diesel-release risk on MPC: correctly identified but overwhelmed by geopolitics. Get the quantitative scan running (the price-data download that the build sandbox blocked) so volume, the 20/50-day moving averages and recent returns are computed rather than scraped. This is a risk-control change, not a return predictor: it reduces how much a single factor shock can swing the episode's results. It is well-founded regardless of this week's sample.

lit.summary: I used all 10 WebSearch calls. The research mostly agrees on a few changes for a weekly momentum list. (a) Stocks with the biggest moves over the last 1–5 days and the last month tend to give some of that back over the next week to month. That is why standard momentum skips the most recent month. Our composite still rewards recent moves through rs_raw (40% weight on the 63-day return, with no skip), accel and breakout, and nothing penalizes a big 1–5 day jump. MTRN (+16% in the 2 days before the pick, then -11.2%) is the textbook case. (b) Two other measures hold up better than raw past return: closeness to the 52-week high (George-Hwang) and residual, volatility-scaled momentum (Blitz-Huij-Martens). The first doesn't reverse later, and the second roughly doubles risk-adjusted profits. Very large single-day gains (the MAX effect) predict underperformance. (c) The S&P 500 inclusion pop has mostly disappeared since about 2010. Additions underperformed by about 1.7pp in their first 21 trading days in the index, so a fresh addition is a fade or watch flag, not a momentum buy. TWLO fits this. (d) Much of momentum is really industry or factor momentum, and momentum crashes come when a crowded group reverses sharply. Several AI-linked names exposed to one news shock is a single bet, not several. A theme cap and volatility-aware sizing are supported. (e) Heavy retail attention (Robinhood herding) predicts negative returns over the next 5–20 days. The WSB "due diligence" signal stopped predicting returns after GameStop. So the social slot should be judged as an attention contrarian or catalyst play, not expected to keep going up. (f) One week of 5 correlated picks says statistically nothing. The episode's pick-average excess return was about -3.8% against SPX, with t ≈ -1.0 even before allowing for correlation between picks. Detecting a realistic edge of 0.3%/week would take roughly 1,600 independent picks, which is years of weeks. Judge rules on the backtest and on 21-day horizons, not on single episodes. Gaps: I didn't confirm the 'frog-in-the-pan' paper, sources on concentration and crowding, or a direct study on sample size through search. The citations for those points come from memory and are flagged where they appear.

findings.title: (1) Short-term reversal: last week's/month's big winners tend to give back gains; momentum works only when the recent month is skipped
findings.detail: Two 1990 papers found the pattern. Lehmann found prior-week winners underperform prior-week losers the next week. Jegadeesh found a 1-month reversal worth about 2%/month (1965-89). That is why academic momentum uses 12-1 (or 2-12) and skips the most recent month. Jegadeesh, Luo, Subrahmanyam & Titman (RFS 2025) model returns that reverse over short horizons and slowly turn into momentum over longer ones. Medhat & Schmeling (CEPR DP15857, 'Short-term momentum') add a key nuance. Last month's low-turnover winners reverse strongly, but last month's high-turnover winners keep going ('short-term momentum'). So a sharp jump isn't automatically bad: one on weak volume is the riskiest, and one on heavy volume is less so. Strength: STRONG for the reversal effect, which is decades old, replicated across markets and part of the standard 12-1 design. Some of the weekly effect is microstructure or lead-lag (Lo-MacKinlay), so it is smaller in large caps after costs. The turnover-conditioned refinement is MODERATE (one published paper plus replications).

(no 1-month skip), config/settings.yaml weights accel 0.05 and breakout 0.05 reward the most recent move. MTRN was +16% in the 2 days before the pick and returned -11.2%.
findings.implication: Add a short-term reversal penalty, or a hard gate, on 5-day and 21-day returns: for example, a percentile penalty when the 5-day return is in the top decile of the universe. Rebuild rs_raw so it skips the last 21 days, or lower its weight relative to mom_12_1. When a stock has jumped a lot recently, condition the penalty on volume: be lenient on high relative volume and harsh on low. Backtest the change at 5-, 10- and 21-day horizons.

findings.title: (2) Extension and large recent gains: a big one-day gain predicts underperformance, while a short moving average sitting above the long one is bullish
findings.detail: Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw (JFE 2011), the MAX effect: stocks with the highest maximum daily return over the past month underperform the lowest-MAX stocks by more than 1%/month, raw and risk-adjusted. Gorman et al. (CFR 2022) argue this is general overreaction rather than lottery preference. Either way, a huge recent up-day is a negative signal. Avramov, Kaplanski & Subrahmanyam (RFE 2021) find a separate, positive signal: when the 21-day moving average is above the 200-day (MAD), returns are higher, with about 9% annualized value-weighted alpha that holds up beyond momentum and the 52-week high. Putting these together: a long-run trend structure (short MA above long MA) is good, while a sharp price spike far above a short MA is a short-horizon risk. The search found no paper that tests price/SMA50 > X% as a pullback predictor directly. The '25-30% above the 50-day' rule is a practitioner heuristic, though it is consistent with MAX and short-term reversal. Strength: MAX is STRONG (JFE, widely replicated; the explanation is debated). MAD is MODERATE (one paper, no independent replication found). Specific extension cutoffs are WEAK (heuristic only).
findings.evidence: https://alphaarchitect.com/hot-off-the-jfe-press-maxing-out-your-returns/ ; https://cfr.ivo-welch.info/published/papers/gorman2021could.pdf ; https://alphaarchitect.com/moving-average-distance/ ; https://anderson-review.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/Avramov-Kaplanski-Subra_2018_SSRN-id3111334.pdf ; repo: config/settings.yaml selection.max_extension 0.25 is measured against the 20-day SMA (features.py:87). The panel overrode the gate for TWLO, which was about 30% above its 50-day; TWLO -8.5% and MTRN -11.2% (about 25% above its 50-day).
findings.implication: Make the extension gate binding: no panel overrides without a written, rule-based exception. Add a MAX feature (largest daily return over 21 days) with a negative weight. Consider adding MAD (SMA21/SMA200) as a positive trend feature, possibly replacing part of trend_template. Backtest whether a cap on extension versus the SMA50 adds anything beyond the SMA20 cap.

findings.title: (3) S&P 500 inclusion: the run-up has mostly disappeared, and additions tend to lag after the effective date
findings.detail: Greenwood & Sammon (NBER w30748): the abnormal return from being added fell from 3.4% (1980s) and 7.6% (1990s) to about 0.8% in the 2010s. The later version calls the post-2010 effect statistically zero. S&P DJI (1995-June 2021): the median excess return from announcement to effective date fell from 8.32% (1995-99) to -0.04% (2011-21). New additions underperformed by about 1.7pp over their first 21 trading days in the index. Patel & Welch (RAPS 2017) find solid evidence that the gains reverted in the 2000s, with no lasting shift in demand. Vijh & Wang (2022) find that 2016-2020 upgrades from the S&P 400 had a 3-day announcement excess return of about -2.5%. Strength: STRONG that the effect has faded (several independent studies plus the index provider's own data). The post-effective underperformance is MODERATE: S&P's own number over a 26-year sample, and the search didn't confirm it separately for 2021 onward.
findings.evidence: https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w30748/w30748.pdf ; https://alphaarchitect.com/disappearing-index-effect/ ; https://www.morningstar.com.au/stocks/investors-can-t-rely-on-the-index-effect-for-a-quick-buck-s-p ; https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/finmgt/v51y2022i4p1127-1164.html ; https://sf.cufe.edu.cn/info/1198/6036.htm (Patel-Welch abstract). TWLO sold off after its inclusion took effect on Oct 6: -8.5%, below the $280 invalidation level.
findings.implication: Add an event flag: any name whose index addition is effective within the pick week, or that rose sharply between announcement and effective date, gets a penalty or is moved out of the momentum slot. Don't treat 'S&P 500 inclusion' as a bullish catalyst in the fact sheet or the script.

findings.title: (4) Momentum crashes and theme concentration: much of momentum is industry or factor momentum, so similar names add up to one bet
findings.detail: Moskowitz & Grinblatt (JF 1999): industry momentum explains much of individual-stock momentum and holds up in large, liquid stocks. Arnott, Clements, Kalesnik & Linnainmaa trace industry momentum largely to factor momentum, i.e. time-varying factor exposure. Daniel & Moskowitz ('Momentum Crashes', JFE 2016): momentum crashes when the market or a crowded group rebounds or reverses sharply, because the portfolio has become concentrated in the recent winners' common exposure. For a 5-name list: if 2-3 names share a theme (AI/semis, AI-infrastructure software, AI materials), one news shock like the OpenAI revenue report hits them together. The effective number of independent bets is closer to 2-3 than 5. The search found no paper specifically on theme caps for small portfolios. The diversification arithmetic is standard portfolio theory. Strength: STRONG that industry or factor exposure drives momentum and crashes. The case for a theme cap specifically is MODERATE: it is inferred from the above, not tested directly.
findings.evidence: https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v54y1999i4p1249-1290.html ; https://rodneywhitecenter.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/Juhani.pdf ; https://alphaarchitect.com/risk-of-momentum-crashes/ ; repo: settings.yaml max_per_sector: 2 uses GICS-style sectors, which miss cross-sector themes (NVDA, TWLO and MTRN all had AI-demand links but sit in different sectors).
findings.implication: Add a theme/correlation cap alongside the sector cap: for example, reject a candidate whose 60-day return correlation with an already-selected pick is above about 0.6, or tag themes (AI-capex, rates, oil) and allow at most 2 per theme. Have the fact sheet report the list's average pairwise correlation and its net exposure to the dominant theme.

findings.title: (5) 52-week-high and residual momentum beat raw momentum
findings.detail: George & Hwang (JF 2004): closeness to the 52-week high predicts returns better than past return (individual or industry), and unlike raw momentum its returns don't reverse long-term. Some critics flag possible data mining in the U.S. sample. Blitz, Huij & Martens (JEF 2011), residual momentum: rank on 12-1 residuals from a 36-month Fama-French 3-factor regression, scaled by residual volatility. This cuts factor exposure and roughly doubles risk-adjusted profits, with more consistency over time. Huij & Lansdorp (2017) confirm it across global universes and out of sample. Residual momentum also directly reduces the theme/factor concentration in finding 4. Strength: STRONG for both (top journals, multiple replications). The 52-week-high effect may have weakened after publication, like most anomalies.
findings.evidence: https://alphaarchitect.com/the-secret-to-momentum-is-the-52-week-high/ ; https://repub.eur.nl/pub/22252 ; https://www.econbiz.de/Record/residual-momentum-blitz-david/10009194616 ; repo: prox_52w_high already weighted at 0.15. There is no residual-momentum feature, and rs/mom_12_1 are raw returns against the benchmark.
findings.implication: Add a residual momentum feature: regress on SPY plus the sector ETF (or the FF factors), take the 12-1 residual and divide by residual volatility. Shift weight from raw rs (0.20) toward it, and keep or increase prox_52w_high. Test in the existing walk-forward optimizer.

findings.title: (6) Volatility-scaled momentum improves risk-adjusted returns and reduces crash risk; the size of the gain is debated
findings.detail: Barroso & Santa-Clara (JFE 2015): momentum's risk is predictable from its own recent realized variance. Scaling to a constant volatility target (about 12%) almost eliminated crashes and nearly doubled the Sharpe ratio. Daniel & Moskowitz (JFE 2016) scale dynamically using forecasts of both mean and variance, and report beating constant-vol scaling. Caveats: Cederburg et al. (2020) find volatility management often hurts real-time performance in general, and Liu et al. (2019) raise look-ahead concerns, though they say the Barroso-Santa-Clara version holds up. For stock selection, the parallel idea is ranking on return divided by volatility (risk-adjusted momentum or residual-vol scaling, as in finding 5), which favors smooth trends over spikes. Strength: MODERATE-STRONG for momentum-factor timing. Risk-adjusted ranking for single-name selection is MODERATE, mostly through the residual-momentum evidence.
findings.evidence: https://alphaarchitect.com/risk-of-momentum-crashes/ ; https://alphaarchitect.com/avoiding-momentum-crashes/ ; https://pureadmin.qub.ac.uk/ws/files/139425062/volatility_scaling_in_momentum_Dec_17.pdf
findings.implication: Rank momentum on volatility-adjusted returns (return / 63-day vol, or residual t-stat), not raw returns. This automatically ranks MTRN-style spikes lower. At the list level, when realized momentum-factor volatility is high, as after this week's AI shock, lean the momentum slot toward lower-beta, lower-volatility leaders. The script should also tell listeners to size names by volatility.

findings.title: (7) Retail attention and social buzz predict short-term underperformance; WSB due diligence stopped predicting returns after GameStop
findings.detail: Barber, Huang, Odean & Schwarz ('Attention-Induced Trading and Returns: Evidence from Robinhood Users', JF 2022): the stocks Robinhood users buy most heavily each day earn about -3% abnormal return over the next 5 days, or about -6% for the most extreme herding events. The UC Davis summary reports about -5% over the next month for top buys and about -9% reversals for the most extreme herding. Barber & Odean (2008): individual investors are net buyers of attention-grabbing stocks, which then underperform. Bradley, Hanousek, Jame & Xiao (RFS 2024): WSB due-diligence buy calls predicted returns before GameStop (about 1.1% 2-day abnormal return, then continued drift), but that predictive power disappeared after GME as posts shifted toward attention and price-pressure names. An Oxford study finds WSB gives little signal outside meme stocks. Strength: STRONG that attention spikes lead to short-term overpricing and reversal (top journals, several datasets). Positive predictive value of buzz is WEAK after 2021. NVDA, the most-discussed mega-cap, returned -1.5% in our social slot.
findings.evidence: https://www.smallake.kr/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/SSRN-id3715077.pdf ; https://gsm.ucdavis.edu/news/what-effect-brokerage-robinhood-having-stock-market ; https://scholars.uky.edu/en/publications/place-your-bets-the-value-of-investment-research-on-reddits-walls/ ; https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:6f3c53d3-f0d6-4232-b3cf-bf1696b200f9/files/dsf268587w ; https://evidenceinvestor.com/post/paying-attention-to-online-buzz-harms-returns-research
findings.implication: Keep the social slot as entertainment and a watchlist item, but change the selection rule. Avoid names at the very peak of mention acceleration, especially after a large price jump. Prefer buzz that is rising from a low base and comes with a fundamental catalyst and technical confirmation. Keep social_weight at or below 0.05 in the composite until data/social_history shows positive 5-21 day predictive power. Test buzz both as a contrarian (negative) signal and as a positive one.

findings.title: (8) Holding horizon and sample size: one week of 5 picks carries essentially no statistical information
findings.detail: The momentum literature measures holding periods in months (3-12), not weeks. At 1 week, short-term reversal (finding 1) works against momentum, so weekly evaluation is the noisiest and least favorable horizon. Arithmetic on Episode 1: pick returns were +10.3, -1.5, -5.5, -8.5 and -11.2 (mean -3.3%, SD about 8.4%), against SPX +0.55%. Excess return about -3.8%, standard error about 3.8%, t about -1.0, and that's before accounting for the picks being correlated through one common AI/rates shock, which reduces the effective sample further. A realistic edge (about 0.3%/week per pick with about 6% weekly idiosyncratic SD) needs roughly (2*6/0.3)^2 ≈ 1,600 independent pick-weeks to reach t=2. That is about 6 years of 5 picks a week, so the walk-forward backtest, not the live record, has to justify the rules. Harvey, Liu & Zhu (RFS 2016) argue that a new signal needs t > 3 because of multiple testing. Strength: STRONG (basic statistics). Note: my searches did not return a source on skill-versus-luck sample size. The Harvey-Liu-Zhu citation is from memory and was not checked in this session.
findings.evidence: Computed from the task's Oct 8 results. Source from memory, not verified by search: Harvey, Liu & Zhu, '...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns', https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2249314 . Repo: config/settings.yaml backtest.primary_horizon: 5 and horizons [5, 10, 21].
findings.implication: Don't change the model weights based on one episode. Track every pick in the ledger at 5-, 10- and 21-day horizons, with excess returns versus SPY and versus an equal-weight momentum benchmark, and judge on rolling 26+ week windows. Consider making 21 days the primary optimization horizon, or blending 5 and 21, since the momentum effect is concentrated there. Only accept new rules (reversal penalty, residual momentum, inclusion flag, theme cap) if they improve walk-forward out-of-sample results, ideally with t > 2-3. In the episode, present Week 1 as noise, not as a verdict.

audit.summary:
I audited the coded rules against what Episode 1 did. The coded model did not pick Episode 1. A web-research panel picked it using a 0-10 rubric (momentum, technical, social_buzz, under_radar, catalyst, risk), so this week's results say nothing about the model's track record.

The picks averaged about -3.3% against +0.55% for the S&P 500, roughly -3.8% excess. Two traits separate the winner from the losers better than anything else: how far each stock sat above its 50-day average, and whether a known event fell inside the holding week.
- TWLO was about 32% above its 50-day, the S&P 500 inclusion took effect Oct 6, and it fell 8.5%.
- MTRN was about 25% above its 50-day after a 16% two-day jump, and it fell 11.2%.
- MPC was about 16% above, NVDA about 7% and CHEF about 8%. MPC rose 10.3%. NVDA (-1.5%) and CHEF (-5.5%) lost much less, and their losses look tied to the market rather than the setup.
- MPC was also the only pick not tied to the AI and high-valuation trade, which is the trade that broke on the OpenAI revenue report.

**(a) Where the manual selection departed from the code:**
- The rubric's "catalyst" score has no counterpart in the code. It gave TWLO's index inclusion a 9 and made TWLO the top-rated name (8.0), even though "sell-the-news" was listed as a risk.
- The panel used a "30%+ above the 50-day" drop rule that is not in the code. It then overrode that rule for TWLO against two fact-checks that recommended swapping in TER.
- The code's own stretch gate (more than 25% above the 20-day average) would probably not have stopped TWLO or MTRN either.
- The social pick, NVDA, was chosen for its chart. It did not have the accelerating mentions that the code's social score mostly rewards.
- The $10B market-cap ceiling for the sleeper slot exists only in the research prompts, not in the code.
- MPC's reference price was Thursday's close, not Friday's.
- The ledger stores rubric scores divided by 10 in its "composite" column, and "composite_rank" holds the order picks were listed in rather than an actual rank. That will distort any later comparison of the model against live results.
- dossier.json does not contain the panel ballots or the final decision record the task mentioned.

**(b) Gaps this week exposed in the coded model:**
- **Short-term reversal:** `ret_1w` is calculated but never scored. Meanwhile `rs` (40% weight on 3-month return), `accel`, `rel_volume` and `breakout` all reward a recent spike.
- **Gap or one-day spike:** there is no filter. `compute_features` does not even read opening prices.
- **Events:** there is no events data at all — no earnings dates, index changes or lockups.
- **Theme concentration:** only the sector cap exists. Its sector data is only fetched in live runs, so in the backtest it never applies.
- **Stretch:** measured against the 20-day average only.
- **Volatility:** no adjustment anywhere. Relative strength, stretch, spikes and stop levels all use raw percentages, which favours volatile names.
- **Social:** no snapshot history exists (there is no `data/social_history`). The backtest never passes social data, so the social slot is silently filled by a fourth momentum name, and the sleeper slot's "low attention" test uses trading volume only.
- **Holding horizon:** the optimizer tunes for a 5-day hold bought at Monday's open. The script tells listeners that buying near Friday's price is "a chase" and to wait for the breakout or a pullback, so the backtest measures a trade the show advises against.

**(c) Code changes and how to validate them:** each finding below names the file and function and gives the backtest test.
- Add the new features to `compute_features`, and the new filters to `select_picks` and `config/settings.yaml`.
- Add a new events module.
- Change `engine.run` so it can take social history, sector data and a correlation matrix, and add an `entry_mode` option.
- Add per-pick diagnostic columns and a paired ablation helper for out-of-sample comparisons.
- In `optimize.py`, take the hard filters from config and add each new score to `PRICE_FEATURES`. Use a small set of filter thresholds chosen in advance, so the weight search doesn't just fit noise.

**Things in the backtest that would mislead the evaluation:**
- **Survivorship and look-ahead:** the backtest universe is today's listed stocks, filtered by today's trading volume. That drops companies that delisted or faded and includes companies that only later became big.
- **Costs:** a flat 10 basis points round trip, regardless of liquidity, filled at Monday's open.
- **Mismatched entry prices:** the scorecard ledger buys at the next open, while this week's results are measured from the reference closes.
- **Beta:** a high-beta set of picks is compared only with SPY, with no beta adjustment.
- **Multiple testing:** the optimizer picks the best of 400 random weight sets per fold and reports no adjustment for that.

One week and five picks is anecdote, not evidence. MPC is a clear counterexample to a blunt short-term reversal penalty: a 6% one-day jump on headlines, and it was the winner. Treat everything here as hypotheses for the backtest to test, not as rules to adopt.

findings.title: (b/c) No volatility normalization: relative strength, stretch, spikes and stop levels all use raw percentages
findings.detail: rs_raw is a raw return blend, so ranking it rewards the most volatile names. Nothing divides by realized volatility. The dossier's invalidation levels aren't volatility-scaled either: MTRN's $285 stop was about 9% below entry and TWLO's $280 about 7%, both hit within 3 sessions, while the code's dossier uses max(sma50, ATR stop). CHANGE: f['vol_63'] = ret1.rolling(63, min_periods=40).std() * sqrt(252); f['rs_vol_adj'] = f['rs_raw'] / f['vol_63']. In scoring.py either add 'rs_va' to PCT_FEATURES with _SOURCE['rs_va'] = 'rs_vol_adj', or switch _SOURCE['rs'] behind a config flag (scoring.rs_source: raw|vol_adj). Also use z-scores instead of % thresholds for the spike and stretch gates.
findings.evidence: src/watchlist/signals/features.py:45 rs_raw; src/watchlist/scoring.py:18 _SOURCE; src/watchlist/episode/dossier.py:78-80 invalidation from sma50/ATR
findings.implication: VALIDATE: add rs_va next to rs and let walk-forward weights choose between them. Report the strategy's Sharpe ratio and beta, not just average excess, since volatility-adjusted ranking mostly helps risk-adjusted returns.

findings.title: (b/c) Social buzz was never validated; the backtest silently fills the social slot with momentum names
findings.detail: data/social_history does not exist (data/ contains only archive, cache and ledger), so social_weight 0.05 and the social slot rest on zero evidence. engine.run calls model.cross_section(d) with no social data, so social_score = 0 and the social branch in select_picks is skipped. The 'fill unfilled slots with momentum' line then gives that slot to a 4th momentum name, and summarize's by_slot never shows a 'social' row. In the backtest the sleeper slot measures attention by dollar volume only (scoring.sleeper), while live runs blend in social attention, so sleeper backtest results don't describe the live rule. take_snapshot only saves when an episode runs, so history builds at one snapshot a week at best.

findings.implication: CHANGE: add a daily scheduled `watchlist snapshot` job that calls take_snapshot. Add an optional `social_history` argument to engine.run: use the latest snapshot on or before each date d with social.load_history, then pass social_frame(...) to cross_section. Have the backtest output a 'social' slot result (or mark it unavailable) instead of silently substituting momentum. Set social_weight to 0 until about 26+ weekly snapshots show a positive correlation (IC) between social_score and next-week returns. Validate as the IC of social_score and the social slot's excess return versus the momentum slot.

findings.title: (b/c) Weekly holding period and Monday-open entry contradict how the show tells listeners to trade
findings.detail: The scripts present levels: buy a close above the pivot or a pullback that holds, and the MPC script says 'Buying up near $420 is a chase'. But the backtest and optimizer score buying Monday's open and selling 5 sessions later (forward_returns; primary_horizon 5). Using the provided closes, a pivot-trigger rule would have changed outcomes: NVDA never closed above $238 (Oct 7 close $237.47), so no entry; MTRN closed $319.18 on Oct 5 above the $314.24 pivot, then reached $277 (about -13%); MPC triggered above $431 and closed $463 (about +7%). Five-day returns are also mostly noise for 3-12 month momentum signals.
findings.evidence: src/watchlist/signals/features.py:104-112 forward_returns; config/settings.yaml backtest.primary_horizon: 5; dossier.json MPC levels.how_to_say; results notes for NVDA/MTRN/MPC
findings.implication: CHANGE: add an entry_mode option to engine.run: 'next_open' (current), 'pivot_close', which enters the first close above pivot_20d within N sessions or skips, and optionally 'stop_at_invalidation', which exits on the first close below the invalidation level or at a time stop of 10 or 21 sessions. Optimize on objective horizon 21 (or a 5/21 blend) while still reporting weekly. Validate each mode over the same out-of-sample folds.

findings.title: (c) Make the backtest able to judge these rules: diagnostics plus paired out-of-sample comparisons
findings.detail: optimize.py only searches nonnegative weights over PRICE_FEATURES for a top-3 momentum basket under the trend and 20-day stretch gates. It can't tune gates, slot rules or correlation limits, and its fast path (evaluate_fast) ignores the sector cap, repeat streaks, the sleeper slot and the social slot. CHANGES: (1) engine.run: add diagnostic columns to each pick row (ret_1w, ret_2d, spike_z, extension_50, ext_atr_50, vol_63, event_flag, max pairwise correlation to the other picks). Add summarize(...)['by_bucket'] with average excess return by quintile of each, a cheap check of whether this week's failure modes are real historically. (2) engine.ablation(prep, cfg, variants: dict[str, dict]): run each set of selection overrides over identical out-of-sample dates and report the mean paired per-week difference in pick_ret, its t-stat, hit rate, drawdown and turnover. (3) optimize.build_arrays: build the gate from every selection.* threshold so evaluate_fast matches select_picks. Optionally add a small grid over 2-3 gate thresholds chosen in each training window. (4) Shrink the final weights toward the defaults (e.g., 0.5*default + 0.5*mean of fold winners). Report how many candidates were searched (401 per fold) so the out-of-sample numbers carry an adjustment for testing that many weight sets.

findings.implication: Adopt a gate only if its paired out-of-sample improvement holds up across horizons and folds. Choose thresholds before looking at results (e.g., 50-day stretch 30%, spike 3 standard deviations) to avoid fitting to one bad week.

findings.title: Backtest flaw: survivorship and look-ahead in the universe
findings.detail: cmd_backtest builds the universe from TODAY's nasdaqtrader listings (base_universe), then keeps the top 3,000 by TODAY's 20-day dollar volume (liquid_tickers on a 45-day pull ending today), then downloads 5+ years of history for those names. download_yfinance also drops tickers with no data (delisted). So the historical universe excludes delisted and bankrupt names and names whose liquidity faded, and includes small names that later grew into liquid winners. That inflates momentum results especially, because it effectively knows which past breakouts survived. The point-in-time dollar-volume check in eligibility() doesn't fix this, because the population itself is chosen with hindsight. audit.py acknowledges the same bias for the 2020 archive.
findings.evidence: src/watchlist/cli.py:84-87; src/watchlist/data/universe.py:75-83 liquid_tickers uses iloc[-1]; src/watchlist/data/prices.py:134 drops tickers with no data; src/watchlist/backtest/audit.py:484 survivorship note
findings.implication: Use a point-in-time universe: historical index membership (e.g., Russell 3000 / S&P 1500 history) or a data source that includes delisted stocks. At minimum, choose the universe by liquidity at the backtest START date, and quantify the bias by comparing results across the two universes. Until then, treat absolute backtest excess as an upper bound.

findings.title: Backtest flaw: entry price and costs are optimistic and don't match the reported scorecard
findings.detail: Costs are a flat 10 basis points round trip for every pick (cost_bps), applied to a fill at Monday's open, which is the most volatile and widest-spread print of the week. MTRN trades about 310-360K shares a day, with a $313/$317 after-hours spread (about 1.3%). The IC and top/bottom-quintile statistics carry no costs at all. Entry conventions also differ: the backtest and Ledger._window_return use the next open, while the results in this task are measured from the episode's reference closes (Friday, and Thursday for MPC). The scorecard the show reads next week will therefore differ from these numbers, and neither matches a level-triggered entry.
findings.evidence: config/settings.yaml backtest.cost_bps: 10; src/watchlist/backtest/engine.py:81,103; src/watchlist/ledger.py:75-95 _window_return (first open after start); dossier.json MTRN risks 'Thin liquidity... wide after-hours spread ($313/$317)'
findings.implication: Model costs by liquidity, e.g., bps = a + b / sqrt(dollar_volume), or a spread estimate from daily high/low prices, plus extra slippage for opening fills. Rerun results at 10, 25 and 50 bps. Use one entry convention for the backtest, the ledger and the on-air scorecard.

findings.title: Backtest flaw: excess return isn't beta-adjusted, and per-pick statistics overstate independence
findings.detail: Picks are high-beta momentum names compared only with SPY (bench_fwd), so 'excess' partly measures beta to the market and to tech. This week the Nasdaq was flat and the S&P 500 +0.6%, while the AI trade fell. hit_rate and beat_benchmark_rate count each pick as independent, but picks in the same week share market moves, so these rates look more reliable than they are. The 10- and 21-day horizons overlap with weekly rebalancing; equity statistics are correctly skipped there, but the per-pick hit rates are still reported.
findings.evidence: src/watchlist/backtest/engine.py:105-106 excess = r_net - b, :153-158 per-pick rates; summarize non_overlapping flag
findings.implication: Add the beta-adjusted return of the weekly pick returns against SPY and QQQ (or SMH) to summarize. Report week-level t-stats and the existing universe_ret comparison as the headline measures, instead of per-pick hit rates.

findings.title: Process: no record of the selection panel's decisions
findings.detail: dossier.json does not contain the panel ballots or the decision record the task mentioned. The only traces of the selection process are TWLO's 'PRODUCER FLAG, EXTENSION GATE' risk note and an MPC do_not_say line mentioning 'the MTRN swap'. Without a log it can't be measured whether overrides (TWLO over TER) help or hurt over time.
findings.evidence: grep across episodes/2026-10-04 for ballot/panel/decision finds only research_method text and the two notes cited; dossier.json lines ~461 and ~803
findings.implication: Have the episode pipeline write candidates, gate pass/fail, rubric scores, the final choice and any override with its reason into dossier.json (episode/dossier.py build_dossier). Track rejected alternates (e.g., TER, CVI) in the ledger with a 'not picked' flag, so overrides can be scored against what they replaced.

lessons.lesson: One week of five correlated picks is not evidence about the strategy. The five picks averaged -3.3% against +0.55% for the S&P 500, about -3.8 points, with t of about -1.0 before allowing for correlation. Because the picks moved together, this was really about two independent bets: energy (MPC) against AI and rising rates (NVDA, TWLO, MTRN and partly CHEF). Detecting a realistic edge of about 0.3% per pick per week would take on the order of 1,600 independent pick-weeks.
lessons.basis: Basic statistics on the Oct 2 to Oct 8 results (SD of about 8.4% across picks). Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2016) on the t-stat a new signal needs; that citation came from memory and was not checked by search.

lessons.lesson: The coded model has no track record yet. Episode 1 was picked by a web-research panel using a 0-10 rubric, and the rubric's 'catalyst' axis has no counterpart in the code. That axis made TWLO the top-rated name because of its index inclusion. Nothing this week can confirm or refute the weights in config/settings.yaml or the composite in scoring.py.
lessons.basis: episodes/2026-10-04/meta.json weights_source = 'research rubric (episode 1, no quant scan)'. dossier.json scores TWLO catalyst at 9 and overall at 8.0. scoring.py PRICE_FEATURES has no catalyst feature.

lessons.lesson: Stocks far above their 50-day average and stocks that just made a sharp jump tend to give some of it back over the next week to month. The two most stretched picks were the two worst: TWLO was about 30% above its 50-day and fell 8.5%; MTRN was about 25% above after a 16% two-day jump with no news and only 1.1-1.3x normal volume, and fell 11.2%. A listener who followed the show's own breakout trigger on MTRN lost about 13%.
lessons.basis: Short-term reversal (Jegadeesh 1990; Lehmann 1990). The MAX effect, where stocks with very large recent daily gains underperform (Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw 2011). Big moves without news tend to reverse (Chan 2003). Low-volume jumps reverse more than high-volume ones (Medhat & Schmeling). This week's own correlation between stretch and return is about -0.5, which is not significant (p around 0.35). The specific 20-30% cutoffs are only a trader's rule of thumb.

lessons.lesson: The coded stretch gate measures the wrong thing and would not have caught this week's problem picks. max_extension=0.25 is measured against the 20-day average (features.py: c / sma20 - 1). On that basis TWLO and MTRN were probably only about 10-13% stretched and would have passed. The 50-day rule the panel actually used exists only in the research prompts, and the panel overrode it for TWLO against two fact-checks.
lessons.basis: Verified in the code: src/watchlist/signals/features.py sets f['extension'] = c / sma20 - 1; config/settings.yaml has selection.max_extension: 0.25; dossier.json TWLO risks[0] holds the 'PRODUCER FLAG, EXTENSION GATE' note.

lessons.lesson: Being added to the S&P 500 is no longer a bullish catalyst, and picking a stock in the week the addition takes effect is a known bad setup. TWLO's inclusion took effect Oct 6. Monday's close was flat to Friday's, and the stock then fell below its $280 invalidation level by Wednesday.
lessons.basis: Greenwood & Sammon (2022) on the disappearing index effect. S&P DJI data showing additions lagged by about 1.7 points over their first 21 days in the index. Patel & Welch (2017). A Weiss alert confirmed the post-inclusion profit-taking.

lessons.lesson: Capping two picks per sector does not control what actually matters, which is a shared theme. NVDA (semis), TWLO (software) and MTRN (materials) sit in different sectors but all carried the AI and interest-rate trade that broke on the OpenAI revenue report. The sector cap also never applies in the backtest, because engine.run calls select_picks without any sector data.
lessons.basis: Momentum is largely driven by industries and shared factors, and it crashes when a crowded group reverses (Moskowitz & Grinblatt 1999; Daniel & Moskowitz 2016). Verified in the code: engine.py calls select_picks(xs, cfg, model.weights, streaks=streaks) with no sectors argument. Note that a theme cap reduces how much one shock can swing a week's results; it is not expected to raise the average return.

lessons.lesson: The winner had a fresh, concrete reason to move and the whole industry was rising with it. MPC's jump came on real fuel-supply news, and the large refiners had all logged 6 straight weekly gains. Momentum that comes with news and with the industry holds up better than a jump with no news. Part of MPC's +10.3% was luck, though: the dossier's main risk (a G7 diesel-reserve release) was swamped when crude rose above $102.
lessons.basis: It matches Chan 2003 and Moskowitz & Grinblatt 1999, but here it rests on one stock. MPC's reference price is the Oct 1 close rather than Oct 2, so its return is not directly comparable to the others.

lessons.lesson: The social-buzz slot is the weakest-founded part of the show. NVDA was chosen for its chart while chatter was 'normal' and sentiment 'neutral'. The code would have ranked it low on buzz. The research says spikes in retail attention predict negative returns over the next 5-20 days, and Reddit 'due diligence' posts stopped predicting returns after GameStop.
lessons.basis: Barber, Huang, Odean & Schwarz (2022) on Robinhood herding; Barber & Odean (2008); Bradley et al. (2024) on WallStreetBets. The data/social_history folder does not exist (confirmed), so the backtest has no buzz data at all.

lessons.lesson: How results are measured matters as much as which stocks are picked. Buying at the reference price gives -3.3%. Following the show's own buy triggers gives about -1.1%, because only MPC and MTRN triggered. The backtest measures buying at Monday's open, which is a trade the script tells listeners not to make ('a chase'). Reference dates are also mixed: MPC uses Oct 1, the others Oct 2.
lessons.basis: The forward_returns docstring in features.py (buy at the next open, sell at close[t+h]); the trigger levels and closes in dossier.json; meta.json shows MPC's price date as 2026-10-01.

lessons.lesson: Several things this week did not separate winners from losers, or could not be judged: price above the average analyst target (MPC, the best pick, was about 11% above it), volume confirmation (mostly no data), and insider selling (never sourced). The losses on NVDA (-1.5%) and CHEF (-5.5%) are ordinary weekly noise; both stayed above their invalidation levels and neither hit its buy trigger.
lessons.basis: candidate_dossiers.json analyst fields; dossier.json do_not_say lists; for NVDA and CHEF, both moves are about 1 to 1.5 standard deviations of a normal week.

refinements.name: Hard 50-day stretch gate, also measured in ATR multiples, with no panel overrides
refinements.change: In features.py add f['extension_50'] = c/sma50 - 1 and f['ext_atr_50'] = (c - sma50)/atr14. In the select_picks base filter add (xs['extension_50'] <= sel.get('max_extension_50', inf)) & (xs['ext_atr_50'] <= sel.get('max_ext_atr', inf)). Mirror this in the optimize.build_arrays gate, and also gate sleeper_score at extension_50 <= 0.15. In settings.yaml set max_extension_50: 0.30 to codify the rule the panel already used. Set max_ext_atr from the historical distribution of pick-day values, not from this week. Any override must be logged and tracked as a shadow comparison.
refinements.rationale: The stretch effect has good research behind it (short-term reversal, the MAX effect) and it is the show's own stated rule. The coded 20-day gate is too loose to catch multi-week runs, and a fixed percentage treats a quiet refiner and a high-beta mid-cap the same.

Then a paired ablation on identical out-of-sample folds with a threshold grid fixed in advance ({0.20, 0.30, 0.40, none}), with the threshold chosen inside each training window and applied to the next test window. Adopt only if the paired improvement is positive at both 5 and 21 days with t > 2 and the cost in turnover is acceptable.

refinements.name: Spike and short-term-reversal control that is lenient on high-volume jumps

Add spike_z = max daily return over 5 days divided by the 63-day standard deviation of daily returns, and a MAX feature (largest daily return over 21 days). Add 'rev_1w' (= -ret_1w) and a negated MAX score to PCT_FEATURES with a default weight of 0, so the optimizer decides whether to use them. Add a hard gate selection.max_spike_z: 3.0 (set in advance) that applies only when rel_volume is below about 1.5, so news-driven, high-volume moves like MPC's are not blocked.

MTRN is the textbook case. Making the gate depend on volume follows Medhat & Schmeling (high-turnover winners keep going) and protects the MPC-type winner.

Optionally cap at 2 the names whose 60-day beta to SMH or QQQ is above 1.5. refinements.name: Event calendar: index-inclusion blackout and earnings flag
refinements.change: New module src/watchlist/data/events.py. It loads earnings dates and a maintained config/index_changes.csv (ticker, index, add/remove, announce_date, effective_date), seeded from the historical S&P 500 changes table. The fact-sheet and script templates should stop presenting an index addition as a bullish catalyst.

Pass social history into engine.run and output a 'social' slot result, or mark it unavailable, instead of silently filling the slot with a fourth momentum name. Selection rule: prefer buzz rising from a low base that comes with a catalyst and a clean chart, and avoid names at peak mention acceleration right after a big price jump. Write the sleeper slot's $10B market-cap ceiling into the code, or stop applying it by hand.

reviews.name: Build the measurement harness first: per-pick diagnostics plus paired out-of-sample comparisons
reviews.reason: This changes no trading rule, so there is nothing to overfit. Every other proposal depends on it. I confirmed in the code that optimize.build_arrays builds its gate only from trend_template and the 20-day extension (optimize.py:38-41). Today the optimizer can't see any new gate, slot rule or correlation cap, so this has to come first. Three additions: (a) set aside a final out-of-sample period (for example the last 12 months) that no ablation touches until every rule decision is made; (b) record every variant tried, so multiple testing can be corrected for; (c) use Newey-West/HAC t-stats whenever the horizon is longer than the rebalance interval (21-day returns sampled every 5 days overlap, so a naive t-stat is inflated about 2x).

reviews.name: Fix the ledger and record-keeping: source tag, shadow picks, persisted overrides, one entry convention
reviews.reason: This is bookkeeping and makes no claim about returns. The current ledger mixes rubric scores into 'composite' (I confirmed the picks.csv rows hold rubric values like 0.8 and 0.667, and rank 5 for CHEF), so any model-versus-live comparison is broken today. One caveat on shadow picks: they are the names the panel chose to research in depth, which is a selected sample. They show whether overrides help, but they are not a random control, so don't pool them with picks when estimating the strategy's edge. Also log every gate failure that was overridden, so override value can be measured directly.

reviews.name: Hard 50-day stretch gate, also measured in ATR multiples, with no panel overrides
reviews.reason: Split this into two parts. (1) 'No panel overrides of a stated gate' is process discipline, not a model change. Adopt it now, since the panel will likely pick again before the scan runs. (2) The quantitative gate has to pass the ablation, and its biggest risk is gutting the edge. The strongest momentum leaders routinely sit 20-40% above their 50-day, and the sleeper slot already gates extension <=0.15 on the 20-day (scoring.py:61). The proposed extension_50 <= 0.15 for sleepers is a much tighter, untested restriction. The ablation must report what share of top-decile composite names each threshold removes, and the average rs and mom_12_1 percentile of picks before and after, not just excess return. The good news: the 0.30 cap would not have excluded MTRN (~25%) and only marginally TWLO (~30%), so it isn't reverse-engineered from this week. That also means this week's evidence for it is close to nil. Set the ATR multiple from a pre-specified grid, not a distribution chosen after the fact. Also compute TWLO's and MTRN's actual 20-day extension rather than relying on the '~10-13%' estimate.

reviews.name: Spike and short-term-reversal control that is lenient on high-volume jumps
reviews.reason: The prior is strong: short-term reversal and MAX are among the best-replicated anomalies, and the code does reward recent moves through rs_raw (40% on r63, features.py:45), accel and breakout. Two overfitting flags. (a) The rel_volume < 1.5 exemption cutoff sits right between MTRN's 1.1-1.3x and MPC's news-day volume, so it looks fitted to this week. Put it on a pre-set grid (for example {1.25, 1.5, 2.0, none}) and choose it inside the training windows. Also, Medhat-Schmeling condition on monthly turnover, not 5-day relative volume, so test the turnover version too. (b) spike_z max_spike_z 3.0 is fine as a pre-set value. The rev_1w and MAX features starting at weight 0 is the right design, but each added feature widens the random weight search (400 candidates), which raises overfitting risk on its own. Report how many dimensions were added. Large-cap weekly reversal is partly microstructure and shrinks after realistic costs, so judge this at 25+ bps.

reviews.name: Theme and correlation cap that actually applies in the backtest
reviews.reason: This is justified as a risk control, and the proposal correctly says it should not be judged on mean return. I confirmed engine.py:95 calls select_picks with no sectors, so max_per_sector does nothing in the backtest. The edge risk: momentum winners are correlated by construction (that is industry and factor momentum). A 0.65 pairwise cap pushes picks further down the composite ranking every week, which lowers momentum exposure. Report the composite rank of the replacement picks and the drop in average mom percentile. The success criteria should be lower weekly SD, smaller worst week and smaller drawdown, with the mean not significantly worse, as proposed. Passing sectors into the backtest requires point-in-time sector classifications, otherwise it leaks. The 0.65 cutoff and the SMH/QQQ beta >1.5 rule are both arbitrary, so pre-specify a small grid.

reviews.name: Event calendar: index-inclusion blackout and earnings flag
reviews.reason: Split this in two. Inclusion: stop treating S&P inclusion as a bullish catalyst in the rubric and the script now. That costs nothing and is backed by the index-effect-decay literature regardless of this week. A hard blackout is fine to test, but additions are rare (~20-30 a year, few in the top composite set), so the backtest will have little power. Don't expect it to reach t > 2, and don't let a null result count as proof either way. Earnings: be careful. The earnings-announcement premium and post-earnings drift are positive anomalies, so a 5-session earnings blackout could remove some of the best momentum continuations. Keep earnings as a disclosure flag, and make it a filter only if the ablation shows it helps. Historical earnings and index-change dates must be point-in-time, using the announce date, to avoid look-ahead.

reviews.name: Rank on residual, volatility-scaled momentum and reduce the weight on recent raw returns
reviews.reason: This has the best literature support of any proposal (Blitz-Huij-Martens, replicated out of sample), and it isn't motivated by this week, so it carries little risk of fitting to one episode. Practical problems: standard residual momentum uses a 36-month regression, but the backtest warm-up is about 400 calendar days (cli.py:82) and the live lookback is 600 days. Either lengthen the history or accept a shorter regression window and say so. Sector-ETF regressions need a point-in-time sector map. Making rs_raw skip the last 21 days would make it nearly collinear with mom_12_1, so test it as a replacement, not an addition. Require improvement across most folds, as proposed, and watch for the optimizer simply rotating weight among collinear momentum variants.

reviews.name: Align the backtest with how the show tells listeners to trade, and lengthen the optimization horizon
reviews.reason: Aligning the measurement convention is correct and doesn't involve fitting. Two cautions. (a) The choice of horizon is itself a researcher degree of freedom. Pre-commit to one (21 days, or a fixed 5/21 blend) before looking at the results, rather than picking whichever horizon makes the new rules look best. 21-day returns sampled weekly overlap, so use HAC standard errors. (b) Pivot-entry and stop rules are path-dependent and add more parameters (N sessions, time stop). Fix N and the stop rule in advance, and report the share of picks actually entered, because a rule that skips most picks can look good on a tiny sample.

reviews.name: Rework the social slot: start recording buzz daily, set its weight to 0, and stop the backtest from silently replacing it
reviews.reason: Collecting data/social_history costs nothing and is the only way the slot can ever be validated. I confirmed the folder doesn't exist. Setting social_weight to 0 until there is evidence is the neutral prior, not a fitted change. Reporting the social slot as unavailable, instead of silently filling it with a fourth momentum name, fixes a real misreport. The selection-rule prose ('rising from a low base with catalyst, avoid peak acceleration') is a hypothesis, not a validated rule. Label it that way, and have the panel apply it consistently so it can be scored later. Don't treat NVDA's -1.5% as evidence for or against this.

reviews.name: Fix backtest flaws that inflate results: survivorship, costs and beta
reviews.reason: Confirmed: cmd_backtest picks the universe from the last 45 days of the current symbol directory (cli.py:81-85), so the backtest is survivorship-biased. Costs are a flat 10 bps. This should be priority 2, not 10. Every gate in proposals 3-7 will otherwise be accepted or rejected on a biased sample. Survivorship bias especially flatters momentum and extension rules, because stretched names that later collapsed and delisted are missing. Run the baseline model under the corrected setup before testing any refinement.

missing: Establish whether the base model has an edge before adding anything. Run the current composite through the corrected (survivorship-free, 25+ bps) walk-forward against simple benchmarks: SPY, an equal-weight top-decile 12-1 momentum portfolio, and QQQ/SMH. If it doesn't beat naive 12-1 momentum, adding gates to it is fine-tuning noise.

Multiple-testing control across the whole package. About 8 rules, each with a threshold grid, will be tested on the same out-of-sample folds. Keep a final holdout untouched until all decisions are made, log the number of trials, and use a deflated Sharpe or Bonferroni/Harvey-Liu-Zhu style bar (t > 3 for brand-new signals, lower for well-replicated ones like residual momentum).

A combined, stacked ablation. Each gate (50-day stretch, ATR stretch, spike, correlation cap, event blackout, sleeper extension_50) may look harmless alone, but together they can push picks far down the composite ranking. Report the cumulative change in the picks' average rs and mom_12_1 percentile and composite rank. That metric directly answers whether the edge has been gutted.
Overlapping-return statistics. With rebalance_every 5 and horizons of 10 or 21 days, use Newey-West/HAC or non-overlapping subsamples for every t-stat in the ablation and optimizer objective.

Near-term process rules for the panel. The sandbox still can't download prices, so Episode 2 will probably be picked by the research panel again. Before then, update the rubric: drop or precisely define the 'catalyst' axis that made TWLO the top pick, treat stated gates as binding, cap picks at 2 per shared theme, and log every candidate and override in a structured form. These are low-cost discipline changes, not model changes.

Confirmation-bias check on the research. The evidence was gathered to explain this week's losers. Also search for evidence against each rule (for example studies where stocks extended near 52-week highs keep outperforming, or where high-volume breakouts continue) before adopting it.

Point-in-time data requirements. Sector maps, index-change announce and effective dates, earnings dates and market cap (for the sleeper's $10B ceiling) all need historical versions, or the new filters will leak future information into the backtest.

Decide the sleeper slot's status explicitly. It has no backtest evidence of its own (an attention proxy built from dollar-volume percentile), and the $10B ceiling is applied by hand. Measure it as its own slot in the ablation, the same way as the social slot.
skeptic.overall: The proposal is unusually disciplined about overfitting. It says plainly that Week 1 (5 correlated, rubric-picked names, t ≈ -1.0, about 2 independent bets) is noise. It ties each rule to prior literature rather than to this week's results, and it routes everything through paired out-of-sample tests. I checked the main code claims: rs_raw puts 40% on r63 with no skip, extension is measured against the 20-day average, the backtest calls select_picks without sectors, the fast-path gate only knows trend_template and the 20-day extension, and the universe is picked from current liquidity. All hold. My main corrections: (1) Move the survivorship and cost fixes (priority 10) up to just after the harness. Otherwise every rule gets validated on a biased sample that especially flatters extension and momentum rules. (2) First show that the base model beats naive 12-1 momentum. (3) Add a final holdout, a trial count and HAC t-stats, because about 8 rules with threshold grids tested on the same folds is itself a multiple-testing problem. (4) Watch for edge-gutting by measuring the picks' momentum exposure after all the gates are stacked, not one gate at a time. (5) A few thresholds look fitted to this week, notably the rel_volume < 1.5 spike exemption that sits right between MTRN and MPC. Put those on pre-set grids. Two things can be adopted now because they are process discipline, not model changes: binding gates with no panel overrides, and dropping index inclusion as a bullish catalyst in the rubric and script. Everything else is keep-but-test-first, except the harness, the ledger, the social-history and weight-0 change, and the backtest-bias fixes, which are plain keeps. I'm dropping none of the refinements. The do_not_change list is sound and should stay as written.
